paragraphs: In the preprint Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation, submitted to arXiv on November 4, an Apple research team introduced HALO. The system lets a humanoid robot use its own cameras and natural-language instructions to find targets, sit, open doors, crouch, crawl and push boxes in indoor spaces that have not been scanned in advance. The project page and code repository are public.

The system divides work into three layers: a vision-language model decomposes instructions roughly every two seconds; a motion generator replans five seconds of whole-body motion at about 3 Hz; and a low-level tracker executes the plan at 50 Hz using depth images and proprioception. Training primarily uses **300 hours of simulated task data from 1,000 procedurally generated homes**, linking language, first-person images and human motion.

The physical platform is a Unitree G1 carrying a Mac mini M4 Pro with 64 GB of memory, with an onboard Jetson Orin NX handling low-level control. The default task orchestrator is a four-bit-quantized Qwen3.6-35B-A3B running locally on the Mac mini, enabling operation without an internet connection. The system can optionally use cloud-model APIs.

The authors tested six single-task categories ten times each in six unmapped real-world environments unseen during training: **360 trials in total, with a mean success rate of 91%**. Success required completing the task without falling or getting stuck. Crouching achieved 100%, sitting 85% and pushing boxes 88%. These results apply to the environments and tasks specified in the paper.

Longer composite tasks proved substantially harder. The team tested three task sequences ten times each in one real-world environment, achieving a mean success rate of 70%. The most complex sequence—crouching, going to a target and pushing a box—succeeded in 50% of trials. Reported failures included the robot’s head orientation leaving a box outside its field of view after crouching, as well as perceptual difficulties involving contact and occlusion. The single-task results therefore do not directly establish competence at arbitrary household tasks.

paragraphs: In a paper formally published in Wind Energy Science on November 3, Sima Hamzeloo and colleagues at the Technical University of Denmark studied **wind-wave interactions during a North Sea storm on December 5, 2015**. COAWST linked WRF, including its large-eddy simulation mode, with SWAN. Validation used RUNE lidar and wave-buoy observations. Peak significant wave height reached 5.77 meters; mean storm wind speeds increased from 21.3 m/s at 40 meters to 26.8 m/s at 247 meters.

Six nested domains extended from 9.9-, 3.3- and 1.1-kilometer mesoscale grids to LES grids refined from 100 to 4 meters. Comparing two-way wind-wave coupling with atmosphere-only runs, LES better matched mean winds below roughly 150 meters but produced excessive vertical shear. Higher up, mesoscale and LES results converged and both overestimated observations. Coupling alone did not significantly improve mean wind speeds in this case.

SWAN driven by LES winds better reproduced significant wave height, with roughly half the root-mean-square error of mesoscale-driven output; peak period and mean wave direction differed less. Coupling also increased velocity variances, covariances and turbulence fluxes as waves modified surface roughness and pressure, informing offshore wind inputs and potential turbine-load modeling.

**The turbulence enhancement lacked direct observational validation**. RUNE lacked corresponding high-frequency turbulence data, while fine-grid results were affected by simulation duration and resolution. Greater accuracy across all storms was therefore not established. The study modeled the marine boundary layer and wind-wave fields, not turbine structural damage or post-collision performance.

paragraphs: [2026 Paper Review | Public Abstract and Model Sections] Zheng et al. studied a 10 MW wind turbine with a rotor diameter of 220 meters and a tower height of 130 meters, analyzing its aerodynamic response when it is in a parked state facing an extreme typhoon inflow. The calculation set eight representative inflow directions based on recent strong typhoon observations, and compared the mean load, load fluctuation, main frequency, surface pressure, and separation flow through a two-stage numerical procedure.

The results show that the loading of the parked wind turbine has a significant directional asymmetry. Some directions are characterized primarily by average loads, while others are dominated by fluctuating responses; it is not possible to judge all wind directions based on a single unified drag coefficient. Concentrated pressure, flow separation on the blade surface, tower wake, and aerodynamic interference between the blades, nacelle, and tower all collectively alter the load distribution.

The paper specifically identifies the remaining aerodynamic risks that exist under the parked protection state, particularly suitable for comparison with studies on yaw error, pitch angle, and parked attitude. It does not simultaneously simulate waves, earthquakes, or mooring failure, and it cannot directly infer that the tower will certainly collapse based on aerodynamic loads. This overview retains the numerical analysis object and boundary conditions; the accompanying figures use the wind turbine, rotor, and model setup from Figure 1 of the paper, avoiding the use of irrelevant wind field photographs.

paragraphs: 【2025 Representative Work Review | Public Abstract】McElman et al. studied the extreme sea conditions of offshore wind farms along the Atlantic coast of the United States, focusing on how to calculate significant wave heights with return periods when tropical cyclones and temperate winter storms occur at the same site. The authors compared numerical back-calculation with univariate extreme value analysis and used block maximum and threshold methods to examine the N-year design values obtained from different data sources and methods.

The results show that there are significant differences in the extreme values provided by the two types of model sea conditions, and factors such as the return period, the distance of the site from the storm's center trajectory, and the analysis of mixed storms as a single distribution all influence the estimation. The study therefore proposes a specialized process for handling the extreme wave heights of tropical cyclones, rather than simply extrapolating the maximum single storm wave from short-term data to long-term design sea conditions.

The paper is directly related to the selection of wave input for fixed or floating wind turbines, but it primarily discusses wave environments and statistical methods, and does not provide a universally applicable safety factor for all platforms. paragraphs: [2025 Team Representative Works Review | Open Paper] Zhao et al. used a pedestrian bridge equipped with a health monitoring system as the verification object, constructing a digital twin framework that integrates real-time computation and visualization. Traditional full-bridge finite element models include a large number of components, and the cost of real-time repeated solving is relatively high; therefore, the authors combined monitoring data, machine learning surrogate models, and modal superposition in a divided manner.

The study used one year of bridge data to train the SAE-Transformer, calculating three-dimensional full-field temperature and thermal stress. The model incorporated sequence-aware embeddings and a SwiGLU activation layer; compared to other deep learning models in the paper, the temperature prediction error was reduced by 39% and the stress error by 45%. The vibration part was reconstructed using sparse sensor data through modal superposition, demonstrating full-field motion displayed at 50 frames per second.

These numbers come from the bridge, training data, and comparison schemes, and do not indicate that any structure can achieve a proportional improvement. paragraphs: [2025 representative team paper retrospective | Abstract of the openly available published paper] Jiang and colleagues propose a mega modular substructure for prefabricated high-rise buildings, placing connected prefabricated modules inside a mega-frame. Besides providing usable space, the modules act as distributed auxiliary masses for vibration control, combining the traditional mega-substructure approach with modular construction.

The author optimizes the inter-module connection parameters based on the concept of tuned mass dampers, taking the average displacement of the main structure as the optimization target. Analysis shows that reasonable connections can simultaneously reduce the responses of multiple modes and achieve better control performance compared to the traditional large-scale sub-structures under comparison. The study also discusses the impact of local failure of module sub-structures, collisions between modules, and collisions between modules and the framework on control performance, rather than only reporting the ideal scenario where always effective connections are valid.

This study belongs to the team of Kaiming Bi in the area of structural vibration control, and is not related to papers on offshore wind turbines or ship collisions. The public report provides an analysis of the feasibility and robustness of the proposed structural system and computational range, which cannot be directly equated to the certification of actual ultra-high-rise engineering. For research tracking, one may note the approach of incorporating connection parameters, distributed mass, multi-stage responses, and collision side effects into the same control system.

paragraphs: [2025 Team Representative Work Review | Public Abstract] Wen et al. used large eddy simulation to compare the aerodynamic performance and wake of vertical-axis wind turbines in four representative atmospheric boundary layers. The author list and institution page confirmed the inclusion of Yong Xia from The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. The paper focuses on the relationship between boundary layer wind shear, installation height, and wake evolution, which falls within the specified team tracking direction and is not classified as collision or multi-hazard research.

The results show that the effect of the boundary layer on aerodynamic performance varies with installation height. A higher wind shear index leads to a greater loss of velocity in the near wake and larger fluctuations in turbulence intensity; increasing the installation height can accelerate the recovery of both. Larger shear or lower installation height also causes the unstable vortex breakdown to occur closer to the rotor. Mode decomposition reveals that the dominant mode frequencies in different boundary layers correspond to twice the wind turbine rotational frequency, revealing the connection between the periodic motion of the blades and the coherent wake.

These results provide mechanistic insights for the selection of turbine height and spacing, but since they are based on four types of inflow, they cannot be used to declare a particular layout as optimal for all sea areas, nor have they validated the failure of typhoons or ship collision loads. The introduction retains the actual object of aerodynamics and wake, not expanding "potential for offshore application" into already deployed engineering facts.

paragraphs: 【2025 Team Representative Works Review | Institutional Author Manuscript】Li et al. studied bidirectional data fusion between infrastructure and users, connecting mobile phone sensors with a pedestrian bridge equipped with a health monitoring system. Fixed sensors are good at continuously recording structural and environmental data, while mobile phones can supplement information on pedestrian location, posture, and dynamic behavior. The coverage and error characteristics of the two types of data are not the same.

The study extracts pedestrian patterns from data on a phone's acceleration, direction, and GPS to generate pedestrian loads and input them into a numerical model of the bridge, calculating the full-field response of the bridge; at the same time, it combines bridge monitoring, phone, and online environmental data to construct a micro-environment related to pedestrian perception and vibration comfort indicators. The authors used a week of field data to test the framework, reporting that the data volume and types have been expanded and that the results have acceptable accuracy.

This achievement discusses the integration of human-in-the-loop mobile IoT with structural monitoring, rather than a verified disaster warning system. Short-term pedestrian bridge tests cannot directly replace long-term verification of large offshore structures, and phone positioning and synchronization errors remain application conditions. paragraphs: [2025 representative paper retrospective | Public abstract] Wiley, Jonkman and Robertson screen the sensitivity of the IEA 15 MW reference wind turbine and UMaine VolturnUS-S platform to input parameters at sites in the Gulf of Maine and Humboldt Bay. The study specifically examines parked or idling conditions during extreme storms under IEC-defined load cases, considering ultimate and fatigue loads separately. It therefore differs from studies restricted to wind speeds during normal power generation.

The aerodynamic–hydrodynamic–servo–elastic model requires a large number of environmental, structural, and computational parameters, each of which has statistical uncertainty or time-varying ranges. The authors used a screening method to identify inputs that are more worthy of further precise quantification, with the results showing that the direction of incident waves, current direction, yaw error, and segmented mooring line lengths may all be major sensitive parameters.

This indicates that the ordering dominated by wind turbulence under normal operating conditions may not apply to parked platforms in severe storms. The paper does not equate the screening ranking directly with failure probability, nor does it prove that only the aforementioned four parameters are important; the conclusions depend on the turbine, the sea area, and the selected design operating conditions. Figure 1 shows the 15 MW turbine actually used in this study and the semi-submersible reference platform, allowing readers to compare the research object.

paragraphs: [2025 representative team paper retrospective | Public abstract] Qin and colleagues propose the cable-pulley self-centering energy-dissipating brace, CP-SCED, to control seismic damage in reinforced-concrete double-column bridge piers. It separates a self-centering system that supplies restoring force, an external friction system that dissipates energy, and a cable-pulley system that adjusts post-yield stiffness, allowing the functions to be tuned separately.

The study first provides the structure, working mechanism, and recovery force model, fabricates simplified specimens for experimental verification, and then conducts analysis of support parameters and bridge piers systems. The results are not solely aimed at achieving zero residual displacement: an "partial self-recovery" scheme that allows a certain amount of static residual deformation achieves a better balance between peak and residual deformation. The summary report states that compared to bare piers, the average peak and residual interlayer displacement angles are reduced by 66.14% and 91.55%, respectively; compared to the traditional SCED scheme, the average base shear force under the recommended support is 93.22% of that.

These ratios come from the combination of bridge piers, parameters, and seismic records analyzed in the paper, and are not guaranteed values for arbitrary bridges. The paper is part of the seismic control research conducted by Kaiming Bi, and it is different from the ship collision conditions; its value lies in demonstrating the clear trade-offs among design choices regarding the restoring force, energy dissipation, and internal force requirements.

paragraphs: [2025 representative team paper retrospective | Open-access paper] Lu and colleagues combine 27 years of Tsing Ma Bridge field monitoring with multiscale finite-element analysis to assess traffic fatigue at component and weld levels. A whole-bridge model provides component stresses, with rainflow counting and Miner's rule used to estimate cumulative damage. A more detailed rib-to-deck weld submodel of the upper orthotropic steel deck considers different wheel-load positions.

Research findings indicate that rail loads dominate fatigue damage in major components, while road loads are more critical for the bridge deck rib-plate welds. The calculated lifespans provided in the paper vary significantly: the estimated lifespan of the most critical rail beam is 536 years, whereas the most critical welds have an estimated lifespan of only 30 years. This suggests that the statement "the overall reserve capacity of all bridge components is sufficient" cannot replace local fatigue inspections of welding details.

The above lifespan is an estimate under corresponding load statistics, stress models, and fatigue rules, and is not an unconditional commitment to the actual engineering residual life. Monitoring data provides long-term traffic inputs and is also used to verify finite element stresses, linking the local detailed model to real bridge evidence. The study focuses on the fatigue evolution under long-term traffic loads.

paragraphs: [2025 Representative Work Review | Public Abstract] Kelly proposed a method for identifying load-driven events using filtered flow acceleration. The low-pass filter scale corresponds to the characteristic response time of the wind turbine and controller, followed by calculating the 99th percentile of acceleration every ten minutes, thereby avoiding small-scale measurement noise dominating the extremes, and without the need to preclassify all events into the same turbulence time waveform.

The study utilized more than fifteen years of high-frequency offshore current observations and compared data at 100 and 160 meters. The results showed that acceleration statistics vary with filtering scale, height, and the inversion at the top of the boundary layer; the maximum extreme acceleration does not have a simple correspondence with the ten-minute average wind speed, and is only weakly related to the wind speed standard deviation. The authors further fitted the tails of the distribution, providing an extreme acceleration curve for the longest 50-year return period, and discussed methods for incorporating observed events into random wind field simulations.

This work adds statistical measures related to structural response time under extreme load inputs, which does not equate to abandoning traditional design loading conditions. The data is from a specific coastal site, and extrapolation to other sea areas is still constrained by sample and model conditions. The accompanying figure is a spectral comparison of different acceleration calculations and filtering methods in the paper, not a photograph of a specific wind disaster site.

paragraphs: [2025 Team Representative Works Review | Public Abstract] Luo, Bi, and Pu re-examine the mechanism of the zero-frequency band gap in seismic metamaterials. Such structures aim to attenuate low-frequency surface waves of earthquakes. Previous works attributed the band gap starting from near zero frequency to the collective behavior of artificial units. The authors selected two typical configurations, namely the fixed barrier and the resonant-type super barrier, and combined analytical and numerical analysis to verify this explanation.

The study suggests that the zero-frequency bandgap is not exclusive to metamaterials. The low-frequency cutoff of the clamped barrier can be explained by rigid boundary conditions; the related phenomena of the resonant barrier are associated with the properties of a "hard upper cover over a soft half-space" layered medium, which cannot support certain lower-order surface wave modes. The paper thus distinguishes three sources: structural boundaries, medium layering, and unit resonance, avoiding automatically interpreting similar dispersion diagrams as arising from the same mechanism.

Its contributions are mainly in clarifying the mechanisms, rather than being an engineering product that has already undergone large-scale site seismic verification. The results are applicable to the assumptions of the barrier and medium discussed in the paper and cannot therefore be used to dismiss the vibration-damping capabilities of all metamaterials. For the team of Kaiming Bi, this representative work demonstrates a research path that involves examining the mechanisms through the dynamics model itself, maintaining a clear thematic distinction from studies on wind turbines or ship collisions.

paragraphs: [2025 representative paper retrospective | Public-abstract guide] Hörteborn and colleagues propose the medium-fidelity STAPS model of ship-traffic collision probability, incorporating maneuverability and motion physics into Monte Carlo simulations and comparing it with the lower-fidelity IWRAP Mk II. The study addresses ship-impact scenarios in bridge design, focusing on how model simplifications alter estimated accident probabilities.

A comparison of the two cases shows that both the duration of the error and the routing layout significantly affect the results. In the baseline scenario, the ship collision probability given by IWRAP Mk II is about 4.5 times that of STAPS. The authors therefore believe that the simpler IWRAP is suitable for early design screening, while STAPS is more appropriate for subsequent stages that require more detailed scenarios.

The multiplier here belongs to the specific case under study and cannot be considered a general reduction factor. In the estimation of collision probability, factors such as how far a ship can continue to navigate after entering an abnormal state, how it is affected by the environment, and whether the route through the bridge area allows for avoidance, may all alter the final collision scenario. The value of the study on ship-bridge and offshore structure collision prevention lies in providing a framework for comparing the accuracy of probabilistic models; it does not replace the calculation of structural collision consequences. A single lower contact probability does not equate to the risk of collapse being satisfied by the criteria.

paragraphs: [Representative paper retrospective | Online in 2024, journal volume in 2025 | Open-access paper] Zhang and colleagues report long-term health-monitoring data from Tsing Ma Bridge for 1997-2022, covering environmental conditions, traffic loads and structural response. The 26-year span allows long-term evolution to be compared, rather than treating a few days of observations as typical of the entire bridge.

The results show that the total traffic load has remained stable since 2007, with the number of road vehicles continuing to increase before the 2020 pandemic; the rate of change of the bridge surface annual maximum temperature is approximately 0.51 degrees Celsius per decade, and the cumulative duration of typhoons during the observation period has shown an increasing trend of about 2.5 hours per year, while the wind speed during the monsoon has decreased and become more dispersed. The bridge surface displacement is mainly influenced by temperature, and the self-vibration frequency has basically remained unchanged over the past 26 years.

These trends are statistical results of this bridge and the analyzed period, and they cannot be directly used to infer the future rate of climate change in the entire region; stable frequency does not replace comprehensive local damage inspections. The paper also introduces updates to the monitoring system and the current status. The paper was published online on 19 August 2024 and is included in the 2025 volume. paragraphs: [2024 Representative Works Review | Public Abstract] Müller et al. used three common boundary layer parameterizations in WRF to simulate the marine typhoon Megi, comparing wind speed, wind shear, and wind direction variations across the rotor height in the eye wall and peripheral regions. All three schemes could reasonably reproduce the track and overall structure, but the local wind field used for load assessment was not entirely consistent.

Median wind speed at hub height differed by up to 15% among the schemes. Although the median simulated wind-shear exponent did not exceed the then commonly used IEC value of 0.11, up to 43.6% of the wind profiles in the eyewall exceeded it. Wind veer was less sensitive to the boundary-layer scheme. Wind shear and veer showed pronounced spatial organization along rainbands, implying that a turbine's location can experience rapid changes in wind profile over a short period.

This study separates the average quantity from the local exceedance probability: a lower median does not rule out strong load segments. The results indicate that sensitivity analysis for specific typhoons and model scenarios cannot be used to conclude that all typhoons have the same shear ratio, nor can differences in meteorological simulations be directly converted into the extent of structural damage. Figure 1 shows the nested computational domain of the paper and its position as the storm moves.
